1-0149-0000.sourceText:
Herr talman! Kollegor! I dag vill jag tala om något fruktansvärt som skakat Sverige. En svensk medborgare och polis, Christian Zedig, har mördats i Köpenhamn i en brutal och meningslös våldshandling. En vanlig semesterkväll och fotbollsfirande förvandlades till en tragedi, och en familj har nu lämnats i stor sorg och saknad. En fru som har förlorat sin man och två barn som har förlorat sin pappa. Våra tankar går till dem, till andra anhöriga, kollegor och vänner.

När våld bryter in skadas tilliten i våra samhällen. I städer, på torg och evenemang runt om i Europa ska vi kunna röra oss fritt utan att känna rädsla. Respekt för lag och ordning är inte bara nationella projekt utan gemensamma europeiska värderingar.

Personer som inte har rätt att vara i Europa ska inte kunna hota vår trygghet. Ytterst handlar det om att försvara våra europeiska värderingar och vårt sätt att leva. Vila i frid.
1-0149-0000.englishText:
Mr Speaker! Colleagues! Today I want to talk about something terrible that shook Sweden. A Swedish citizen and police officer, Christian Zedig, has been murdered in Copenhagen in a brutal and senseless act of violence. An ordinary holiday evening and football celebration turned into a tragedy, and a family has now been left in great sadness and loss. A wife who has lost her husband and two children who have lost their father. Our thoughts go out to them, to other relatives, colleagues and friends.

When violence breaks out, trust in our communities is damaged. In cities, in squares and events around Europe, we should be able to move freely without feeling fear. Respect for law and order is not only a national project but common European values.

People who do not have the right to be in Europe should not be able to threaten our security. Ultimately, it is about defending our European values ​​and our way of life. Rest in peace.

1-0150-0000.sourceText:
Signor Presidente, onorevoli colleghi, quante altre vittime serviranno, prima che l'Europa trovi il coraggio di guardare la realtà negli occhi? Quante ancora?

A Milano, un uomo di 55 anni è stato accoltellato oltre 20 volte mentre faceva colazione con il padre. L'aggressore, un giovane nato in Italia da genitori gambiani, dopo l'arresto ha dichiarato: "Mi sono divertito. Appena esco, lo rifaccio".

In Svezia, un poliziotto di 32 anni è stato assassinato da un uomo di origine africana con precedenti penali mentre guardava una partita dei Mondiali.

Sono il volto di un'Europa che per troppo tempo ha preferito voltarsi dall'altra parte.

In troppi casi, gli autori di queste violenze sono giovani nati o cresciuti in Europa, figli dell'immigrazione. La verità è che l'integrazione non si proclama, si costruisce e quando fallisce, il prezzo lo pagano i cittadini innocenti.

Per anni ci hanno detto che bastava accogliere, che tutto si sarebbe risolto da solo, che denunciare questi problemi era intolleranza. Oggi sono i fatti a smentire questa ideologia.

Ma adesso non basta più parlare solo di fermare l'immigrazione illegale, è arrivato il momento di parlare di remigrazione: l'Unione europea deve organizzare una vera politica europea di remigrazione, anche attraverso Frontex.

Per anni abbiamo visto le navi impegnate a portare i migranti in Europa. Adesso dobbiamo invertire la rotta. I mezzi e le risorse europee devono essere utilizzati anche per riportare nei paesi di origine chi non ha il diritto di restare sul nostro territorio. Le espulsioni devono essere eseguite davvero. La remigrazione deve diventare una priorità per la politica europea.

Per troppo tempo l'Europa si è preoccupata di non offendere nessuno anziché di proteggere i propri cittadini, ma la prima libertà è vivere senza paura, il primo diritto è la sicurezza e il primo dovere di uno Stato è proteggere il proprio popolo.

È tempo di proteggere i nostri confini, le nostre città, i nostri cittadini: è tempo di invertire la rotta.
1-0150-0000.englishText:
Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, how many more victims will it take before Europe finds the courage to look reality in the eye? How many more?

In Milan, a 55 year-old man was stabbed over 20 times while having breakfast with his father. The attacker, a young man born in Italy to Gambian parents, declared after his arrest: "I had fun. As soon as I get out, I'll do it again."

In Sweden, a 32 year-old policeman was murdered by a man of African descent with a criminal record while watching a World Cup match.

They are the face of a Europe that for too long has preferred to look the other way.

In too many cases, the perpetrators of this violence are young people born or raised in Europe, children of immigration. The truth is that integration is not proclaimed, it is built and when it fails, innocent citizens pay the price.

For years they told us that it was enough to welcome, that everything would resolve itself, that reporting these problems was intolerance. Today the facts deny this ideology.

But now it is no longer enough to just talk about stopping illegal immigration, the time has come to talk about remigration: the European Union must organize a true European remigration policy, also through Frontex.

For years we have seen ships busy bringing migrants to Europe. Now we need to reverse course. European means and resources must also be used to bring back to their countries of origin those who do not have the right to remain on our territory. The expulsions really need to be carried out. Remigration must become a priority for European politics.

For too long Europe has been concerned with not offending anyone rather than protecting its citizens, but the first freedom is to live without fear, the first right is security and the first duty of a State is to protect its people.

It's time to protect our borders, our cities, our citizens: it's time to reverse course.

1-0151-0000.sourceText:
Signor Presidente, onorevoli colleghi, il tema della sicurezza pubblica in Europa merita certamente la massima attenzione ed è una grande emergenza in alcune aree del mio paese – dell'Italia – in particolare per quanto riguarda la lotta alla criminalità organizzata e alle mafie, ancora forti e presenti sul territorio.

La mia regione è la Sicilia, la terra di Giovanni Falcone e di Paolo Borsellino, di tante donne e uomini che hanno dato la loro vita per combattere la mafia e affermare la legalità.

In particolare, negli ultimi mesi, la mia città – Palermo – ha registrato numerosi episodi di violenza legati al fenomeno mafioso: diversi esercizi commerciali hanno subito violenti atti intimidatori, alcuni sono stati dati alle fiamme e più volte la criminalità organizzata ha sparato con fucili d'assalto, meglio conosciuti come kalashnikov, per intimorire gli onesti imprenditori e indurli a sottomettersi alla logica mafiosa.

A qualche imprenditore è stata recentemente assegnata la scorta per ragioni di sicurezza e incolumità personali, così come recentemente accaduto ad amministratori locali, per ultimo un assessore del mio comune, Palermo.

Dinanzi a tutto ciò, la risposta del governo Meloni è stata fin qui, a mio avviso, del tutto insoddisfacente. Il ministro Piantedosi ha annunciato il rafforzamento di un sistema di videocamere, ma attendiamo misure concrete per il potenziamento degli organici delle forze dell'ordine e della magistratura, per un'efficace contrasto alla criminalità mafiosa, che estende i suoi affari criminali in tutta Europa.

Anche per questo – concludo – mi auguro che la direttiva riguardante il recupero e la confisca dei beni venga presto recepita da tutti gli Stati membri, in modo da produrre risultati efficaci, così come li ha prodotti in Italia la legge La Torre sulla confisca dei beni confiscati alla mafia.
1-0151-0000.englishText:
Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, the issue of public security in Europe certainly deserves the utmost attention and is a major emergency in some areas of my country - Italy - in particular with regard to the fight against organized crime and mafias, which are still strong and present in the area.

My region is Sicily, the land of Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino, of many women and men who gave their lives to fight the mafia and affirm legality.

In particular, in recent months, my city - Palermo - has recorded numerous episodes of violence linked to the mafia phenomenon: several commercial businesses have suffered violent acts of intimidation, some have been set on fire and organized crime has repeatedly fired assault rifles, better known as Kalashnikovs, to intimidate honest entrepreneurs and induce them to submit to the mafia's logic.

Some entrepreneurs have recently been assigned the escort for reasons of personal safety and security, as recently happened to local administrators, most recently a councilor of my municipality, Palermo.

Faced with all this, the Meloni government's response so far has been, in my opinion, completely unsatisfactory. Minister Piantedosi has announced the strengthening of a video camera system, but we are waiting for concrete measures to strengthen the staff of the police and the judiciary, for an effective fight against mafia crime, which extends its criminal affairs throughout Europe.

Also for this reason - I conclude - I hope that the directive concerning the recovery and confiscation of assets will soon be implemented by all member states, in order to produce effective results, just as the La Torre law on the confiscation of assets confiscated from the mafia has produced them in Italy.

1-0152-0000.sourceText:
Herr talman! Det kunde ha varit jag. En fin sommarkväll i Köpenhamn: öl, kompisar, VM på storbildsskärm – svårt att tänka mig något bättre. Det var så kvällen var tänkt för Christian Zedig. Han var 32 år, pappa till två små barn och polis. Han var ledig den dagen. Han försökte bara lugna ner ett bråk, och det var då invandrargänget gav sig på honom. Han slogs ner och stampades på huvudet gång på gång. Han dödades för att han var den som tog ansvar.

Herr talman! Samma vecka knivhuggs en oskyldig man i Milano 20 gånger av en gambiansk invandrare. Gerardo åt frukost med sin far på ett kafé och det kunde ha varit vem som helst av oss här inne. Två attacker i två länder, men samma fråga som vi inte längre kan blunda för. När sådana här saker händer gång på gång, då måste vi våga tala om det.

Ändå röstade socialdemokrater, vänstern och de gröna emot att Europaparlamentet ens skulle få hålla en debatt om de här attackerna och vad de betyder för säkerheten i Europa. Ni rödgröna vill inte ens diskutera det, och det var ni som inte ens kunde ställa er bakom återvändandeförordningen – en lag som kommer att göra det enklare att skicka hem utländska våldsverkare som begår allvarliga brott här i Europa.

Ni säger nej till att tala om problemen. Ni säger nej till att göra någonting åt det. Det här är inte ett politiskt spel, det här är på riktigt. Bakom varje attack finns en familj som aldrig mer blir densamma. Det finns barn som förlorar sin pappa. Vi är skyldiga Christian, Gerardo och alla offer mer än tomma ord. Vi är skyldiga dem handling.
1-0152-0000.englishText:
Mr Speaker! It could have been me. A nice summer evening in Copenhagen: beer, friends, WC on the big screen - hard to imagine anything better. That was how the evening was meant for Christian Zedig. He was 32 years old, the father of two small children and a police officer. He was off that day. He was just trying to calm down a fight, and that's when the immigrant gang turned on him. He was knocked down and stomped on the head repeatedly. He was killed because he was the one who took responsibility.

Mr Speaker! In the same week, an innocent man in Milan was stabbed 20 times by a Gambian immigrant. Gerardo was having breakfast with his father in a cafe and it could have been any of us in here. Two attacks in two countries, but the same issue that we can no longer turn a blind eye to. When things like this happen again and again, then we have to dare to speak about it.

Yet the Social Democrats, the Left and the Greens voted against allowing the European Parliament to even hold a debate on these attacks and what they mean for security in Europe. You red-greens don't even want to discuss it, and you were the ones who couldn't even get behind the return regulation - a law that will make it easier to send foreign violent criminals who commit serious crimes here in Europe.

You refuse to talk about the problems. You refuse to do anything about it. This is not a political game, this is real. Behind every attack is a family that will never be the same again. There are children who lose their father. We owe Christian, Gerardo and all the victims more than empty words. We owe them action.

1-0153-0000.sourceText:
Herr talman! Fotbolls-VM ska vara en folkfest, en plats för glädje, gemenskap och hopp. Istället reste en svensk fotbollssupporter för att uppleva fotboll och kom aldrig hem. Till Christians familj och vänner vill jag uttrycka min djupaste sorg och mitt varmaste deltagande. Må ni finna tröst och ljus i denna bottenlösa sorg.

När ett sådant här fruktansvärt brott sker väcks ilska, sorg och rädsla. Det är bara mänskligt, men det är just i sådana fall och stunder som rättsstaten prövas. Vi som politiker är inte domarna. Vi är inte åklagarna, och vi är inte de som avgör skuld eller straff. Vi är lagstiftare. Vårt ansvar är att se till att människor kan leva i trygghet, att ge polis och rättsväsende de verktyg som behövs för att förebygga, utreda och lagföra dem som begår brotten, och att försvara rättsstaten även när känslorna är som starkast.

Det är därför det är så anmärkningsvärt att Charlie Weimers från Sverigedemokraterna ännu en gång väljer att använda en enskild människas tragiska död för att vinna politiska poänger. När ett pågående brottsfall blir ett politiskt slagträ flyttas fokus från offret och blir retorisk rekvisita. Christian förtjänar bättre. Hans familj förtjänar bättre och den här kammaren förtjänar bättre.

Den här kammaren kan mer än den här nivån. Låt rättsväsendet göra sitt arbete. Låt oss hedra Christian med respekt och inte använda hans minne som politisk rekvisita. Låt oss vara de lagstiftare som våra medborgare förväntar sig att vi ska vara: principfasta, ansvarstagande och värdiga det förtroende de har gett oss.
1-0153-0000.englishText:
Mr Speaker! The World Cup should be a public celebration, a place for joy, community and hope. Instead, a Swedish football supporter traveled to experience football and never came home. To Christian's family and friends, I want to express my deepest sorrow and my warmest sympathy. May you find comfort and light in this bottomless sorrow.

When a terrible crime like this happens, anger, sadness and fear are aroused. It is only human, but it is precisely in such cases and moments that the rule of law is tested. We as politicians are not the judges. We are not the prosecutors, and we are not the ones to determine guilt or punishment. We are legislators. Our responsibility is to ensure that people can live in safety, to give the police and justice system the tools they need to prevent, investigate and prosecute those who commit the crimes, and to defend the rule of law even when emotions are at their strongest.

That is why it is so remarkable that Charlie Weimers of the Sweden Democrats once again chooses to use the tragic death of an individual to score political points. When an ongoing criminal case becomes a political bat, the focus shifts from the victim and becomes a rhetorical prop. Christian deserves better. His family deserves better and this House deserves better.

This chamber is capable of more than this level. Let the judiciary do its job. Let's honor Christian with respect and not use his memory as a political prop. Let us be the legislators our citizens expect us to be: principled, accountable and worthy of the trust they have placed in us.

1-0154-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident! 80 Messerstechereien am Tag, über 1 000 Tote im Jahr – das ist die Situation in Deutschland. Wir reden aber heute über Italien und Dänemark. Über Deutschland reden wir gar nicht mehr, weil wir uns an die Gewalt gewöhnt haben. Solingen, Mannheim, Aschaffenburg, Polizisten, Zugbegleiter, Kinder – überall in Deutschland werden unschuldige Menschen Opfer sinnloser Gewalt. Aber nicht nur Messer kommen dabei zum Einsatz, sondern immer öfter auch Schusswaffen; jeden Tag gibt es Schießereien in Berlin. In Stade in Niedersachsen wurden vor einer Woche sechs Menschen erschossen, in einem Mutter‑Kind‑Heim – kaltblütig ermordet, weil sie einem Kind helfen wollten.

Wer sind die Täter? Auch hier ist die polizeiliche Kriminalstatistik eindeutig: Bei schweren Gewaltdelikten sind Syrer und Afghanen zehnmal häufiger Tatverdächtige als Deutsche. Kriminelle syrische Clans machen sich in Dortmund, Bremen oder Berlin breit mit massiver Gewalt.

Ich frage Sie: Wie kann es sein, dass Menschen, die angeblich vor einem Krieg geflüchtet sind, bei uns kriminell werden? Wie kann es sein, dass Menschen, die von uns alles bekommen – Wohnung, Bürgergeld, Krankenversicherung; über die Hälfte der Syrer lebt in Deutschland vom Bürgergeld –, wie kann es sein, dass diese Menschen bei uns morden, rauben und vergewaltigen?

Weil sie eine andere Kultur haben. Weil sie unsere Großzügigkeit für Schwäche halten, und weil sie ihre Familienehre über unser Recht und unser Gesetz stellen.

Es gibt deshalb nur eine Antwort auf die eskalierende Gewalt: Remigration. Wir müssen diese Leute in ihre Heimat zurückbringen. Wer angegriffen wird, muss sich verteidigen.
1-0154-0000.englishText:
Mr. President! 80 stabbings a day, over 1,000 deaths a year – that is the situation in Germany. But today we're talking about Italy and Denmark. We don't even talk about Germany anymore because we've gotten used to the violence. Solingen, Mannheim, Aschaffenburg, police officers, train attendants, children - all over Germany, innocent people are becoming victims of senseless violence. But not only knives are used, but also firearms more and more often; There are shootings in Berlin every day. In Stade in Lower Saxony, six people were shot a week ago in a mother and child home - murdered in cold blood because they wanted to help a child.

Who are the perpetrators? Here too, the police crime statistics are clear: Syrians and Afghans are ten times more likely to be suspects in serious violent crimes than Germans. Criminal Syrian clans are spreading massive violence in Dortmund, Bremen and Berlin.

I ask you: How can it be that people who supposedly fled a war become criminals here? How can it be that people who get everything from us – housing, citizens’ benefit, health insurance; Over half of the Syrians in Germany live on citizens' money - how can it be that these people murder, rob and rape here?

Because they have a different culture. Because they consider our generosity to be weakness, and because they put their family honor above our justice and our law.

There is therefore only one answer to the escalating violence: remigration. We have to return these people to their homeland. Anyone who is attacked must defend themselves.

1-0155-0000.sourceText:
Herr Präsident! Ich war mir fast sicher, dass es dazu kommen würde, Herr Sell; ich hätte wirklich ein Monatsgehalt darauf gewettet.

Herr Präsident, ich möchte mich zur Ausführung der rechtlichen Analyse, warum das hier ein Verstoß gegen Artikel 10 Absatz 3 und Artikel 10 Absatz 4 der Geschäftsordnung ist, des Rechtsvergleichs bedienen. Der Kollege Weimers, der hat Sachen gesagt, denen ich vielleicht nicht in allem folgen kann, die sich aber im Rahmen einer respektvollen Auseinandersetzung bewegen. Der Kollege Sell hat gesagt, dass diese Menschen rauben, morden und vergewaltigen, weil sie eine andere Kultur haben. Das war die Aussage.

Das ist der Unterschied zwischen einer harten politischen Auseinandersetzung und rassistischen Ausfällen, und das ist das, was wir hier in diesem Haus nicht tolerieren können. Deswegen bitte ich Sie und das Präsidium – können Sie mal bitte den Mund halten, wenn ich rede, Herr Jungbluth? Deswegen bitte ich Sie, dem entgegenzutreten, das zu prüfen, denn bei aller berechtigten Sorge, bei aller berechtigten Wut kann in diesem Haus nicht, weil Menschen ermordet werden, Platz für Rassismus sein.
1-0155-0000.englishText:
Mr. President! I was almost certain that it would happen, Mr. Sell; I really would have bet a month's salary on it.

Mr President, I would like to use legal comparison to carry out the legal analysis of why this is a breach of Rules 10(3) and 10(4) of the Rules of Procedure. My colleague Weimers said things that I may not be able to fully follow, but that are part of a respectful debate. Mr Sell said that these people rob, murder and rape because they have a different culture. That was the statement.

That is the difference between a tough political debate and racist abuse, and that is what we cannot tolerate in this House. That's why I ask you and the Presidium - can you please keep your mouth shut when I'm talking, Mr. Jungbluth? That's why I ask you to confront this, to examine it, because despite all the justified concern, despite all the justified anger, there can be no room for racism in this House because people are being murdered.
